name: Neo-Ottomanism
summary: Neo-Ottomanism is a Turkish current that seeks to reconcile the republic with its Ottoman, Islamic and multinational past and to use that heritage to make Turkey an active, self-confident power in the regions the empire once ruled: the Balkans, the Caucasus and the Middle East. Its defining scholarship describes it as favouring a moderate secularism with a larger public role for Islam, a less ethnic, more multicultural citizenship open to Kurdish cultural rights, a market economy, and soft power, trade and mediation abroad while keeping Turkey's NATO and EU ties. Its best-known statement, Ahmet Davutoglu's strategic depth doctrine and zero problems with neighbours policy, adds economic interdependence and support for democratic change, though Davutoglu himself rejects the neo-Ottoman label.
scope: As the defining scholarship sets it out: Taspinar (s5) defines neo-Ottomanism by three traits (coming to terms with the Ottoman and Islamic heritage with moderate secularism and Kurdish cultural rights; grandeur and soft power in former Ottoman lands; embracing the West as much as the Islamic world) and names Turgut Ozal as its early proponent and Davutoglu's strategic depth as its AKP-era form; Murinson (s6) and Carlucci and Ennas (s7) trace the same line from Ozal's circle (Cengiz Candar) to Davutoglu, and Grigoriadis (s8) discusses Davutoglu's doctrine as the one often called neo-Ottomanism. The profile answers from these accounts and from Davutoglu's own texts (s10-s12), which they tie to the ideology. Neo-Ottomanism was never the declared doctrine of the Turkish state (its main theorist rejects the label), so it has no state record of its own and every answer rests on words; AKP government practice, Erdogan's later militarised policy, pan-Turkism, Ottoman dynastic restorationism and the Gulen movement are other subjects.

central-planning.rationale: The ideology Murinson describes rests on laissez-faire economics, state non-intervention and the market-friendly Islam of the Anatolian business class, the opposite of a planned economy.

close-ties-china.rationale: Grigoriadis reports Davutoglu's view that close relations with all rising powers, China, India, Russia and Brazil, are key, within a multi-dimensional policy not tied to one partner.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Davutoglu's 2013 article backs the Arab uprisings as a struggle for reinstituting popular sovereignty as the basis of political authority.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Davutoglu rejected the Swiss minaret referendum on the ground that fundamental religious rights must not be subject to a popular vote, so a majority may not decide them.

democracy-best.rationale: Davutoglu calls democracy Turkey's most important soft power and says Turkey must deepen and enrich it; Taspinar lists a democratic political system among what the ideology projects abroad.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Davutoglu makes cultural coexistence and plurality a principle of regional order, saying no Middle Eastern city was ever homogeneous and that this composition must be maintained.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Davutoglu states that order cannot be achieved in an atmosphere of isolated economies and promotes free trade and energy corridors with all neighbours, against any closed economic bloc.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Davutoglu's first principle is a balance between security and freedom: administrations that restrict liberties for security become authoritarian, and Turkey fought the PKK without declaring a state of emergency or narrowing liberties.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Davutoglu counts the strategic relationship with the United States and NATO membership as an integral part of Turkey's multi-dimensional policy.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: In Sarajevo Davutoglu called it a mistake to put a fundamental religious right to a popular vote, arguing that human rights could not have spread had freedoms been put to referenda.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Taspinar writes that neo-Ottomanism, at peace with Turkey's multinational legacy, opens the door to a less ethnic and more multicultural conception of citizenship.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: This is the ideology's core: Carlucci and Ennas define neo-Ottomanism as promoting greater Turkish engagement in all former Ottoman regions, and Taspinar and Murinson describe soft-power influence in former Ottoman territories.

free-trade.rationale: Davutoglu's essay makes economic interdependence a principle of regional order and holds up the Syria free trade agreement, which integrated the two economies, as a model.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: Davutoglu argues that order in the Middle East cannot be built among isolated economies and counts economic interdependence among the foundations of regional security; Taspinar notes Ozal's matching vision of peace through economic interdependence.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: Davutoglu's Sarajevo address commits Turkey to the Alliance of Civilizations to promote dialogue and respect for diversity, and Grigoriadis reports he made intercivilisational dialogue a leading priority.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Davutoglu wants the region's peoples to enjoy the same universally acknowledged rights as their peers elsewhere, and Taspinar describes the ideology as presenting Turkey as proof that Islam and democracy are compatible.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Taspinar describes neo-Ottomanism as embracing the West as much as the Islamic world and presenting Turkey as proof of the compatibility of Islam, democracy and secularism.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Taspinar states that neo-Ottomanism does not seek to institute an Islamic legal system in modern Turkey.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Murinson describes neo-Ottomanism as the ideology of the new Anatolian elite, one that emphasizes small business, laissez-faire economics and state non-intervention; Taspinar lists a capitalist economy among the strengths it projects.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Grigoriadis reports that Davutoglu wants Turkey to put aside the militaristic image left by its history of military tutelage over society and politics.

minority-language-support.rationale: Taspinar writes that neo-Ottomanism is open to cultural rights for Kurds and sees no threat in them, and that Ozal was an early supporter of Kurdish cultural rights.

more-religion-public.rationale: Taspinar says neo-Ottomanism gives Islam more political space and a greater role in shared identity, Murinson that it gives Islam a prominent place, and Carlucci and Ennas that Ozal enabled Islam to regain a public role.

national-mission.rationale: Murinson sums up the spirit of neo-Ottomanism as Turks feeling called to lead other Muslim nations toward representative democracy and modernity.

national-self-determination.rationale: Davutoglu insists on Iraq's territorial integrity and unity against the formation of new states from it, and Taspinar describes Kurdish rights as accepted within loyalty to the Republic.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Davutoglu says Turkey should pursue EU accession even if the EU freezes relations and that Europe's power needs Turkey's full integration; Taspinar notes Ozal applied for membership.

population-transfer.rationale: Taspinar writes that neo-Ottomanism seeks to accommodate and co-opt the Kurds within a multicultural citizenship, and Davutoglu insists the region's mixed population be maintained.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Taspinar's first defining trait of neo-Ottomanism is coming to terms with Turkey's Ottoman and Islamic heritage at home, and Carlucci and Ennas describe its projection of that heritage abroad.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Davutoglu writes that Turkey chose to support the popular uprisings for basic democratic rights and urged the region's rulers to make democratic reforms, refusing to accept that others be denied the rights the Turkish people enjoy.

public-ownership.rationale: Murinson's account of the ideology's economic side is laissez-faire economics and state non-intervention, which leaves no place for public ownership of major industries.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Taspinar contrasts the neo-Ottoman view of the headscarf as a matter of individual religious freedom with the Kemalists' strict measures against headscarves.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: Davutoglu holds that the mixed ethnic and sectarian make-up of the region's cities must be maintained, and Taspinar describes a multicultural citizenship open to Kurds.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Taspinar describes neo-Ottomanism as a pragmatic mindset that seeks to co-opt rather than confront, and Davutoglu presents its energy policy as a rational calculation, not an ideological account.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Taspinar writes that neo-Ottomanism pursues no policy of resurrecting the Ottoman Empire and does not question the nation-state and the achievements of the republic.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Davutoglu cites development assistance, a campaign for Somali famine victims and attention to the least-developed countries as cornerstones of Turkey's foreign policy.

right-to-secede.rationale: Davutoglu treats Iraq's disintegration as a danger and backs its territorial integrity, and Taspinar says Kurdish identity is accepted only as long as Kurds stay loyal to the Republic of Turkey.

separate-church-state.rationale: Taspinar writes that the ideology favours a more moderate secularism in place of the militant laicism of the Kemalist regime, and Murinson that it negates the secular Kemalist legacy.

single-official-language.rationale: Taspinar sets the neo-Ottoman acceptance of Kurdish cultural and language rights against the Kemalist view that even the Kurdish language is dangerous to assimilation.

state-harmful.rationale: Taspinar writes that neo-Ottomanism shares with Kemalism a strong attachment to the Turkish nation-state and a state-centric view of the world.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Taspinar writes that the AKP's neo-Ottoman leaders reach East to complement their ties to the West, not replace them, and Davutoglu keeps NATO at the core of Turkey's position.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The defining sources point both ways: Taspinar says it seeks influence, not imperialism or a resurrected empire, while Murinson treats soft power as an interim choice and Carlucci and Ennas describe a later militarised form.

missingStatements.text: A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.
missingStatements.rationale: Greater Turkish engagement in former Ottoman regions (Balkans, Caucasus, Middle East) is the defining goal of the ideology, though Davutoğlu frames it as soft power.

missingStatements.text: A historic building that serves as a museum may be converted back into a place of worship.
missingStatements.rationale: The 2020 Hagia Sophia and Chora conversions are the signature symbolic act of the movement.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-09), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-16) rested mostly on two Wikipedia articles (s1, s4), a third-party copy of Davutoglu's 2008 essay (s2) and a Wilson Center profile (s3); under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence, so every first-pass answer was checked against the defining sources and changed or nulled (166 nulled), with the first version kept in each statement's reviewHistory. This pass read in full Taspinar's Carnegie paper (s5), Murinson's BESA monograph (s6), the neo-Ottoman sections of Carlucci and Ennas (s7), Grigoriadis's ELIAMEP paper (s8) and three texts by Davutoglu (s10-s12). Themes searched: world (alliances, EU, neighbours, Iraq, territorial claims), government (democracy, security and freedom, military tutelage, referenda), society and culture (Islam and secularism, headscarf, Kurdish rights, multiculturalism), economy (markets, trade). The defining sources say almost nothing on welfare, taxation, labour, family, sexuality, ecology or technology; those statements are null. Hristov's 2019 article in Social Evolution & History was read and left out (it rests on conspiracy claims about 'Anglo-Saxon and Jewish elites'); Insight Turkey and the Open University repository (Wastnidge 2019) refuse scripted access; Yavuz's Nostalgia for the Empire (2020) and Murinson's 2006 article are not open access. The old missing statement on former-empire influence now cites s5 and s7 instead of s1 and the third-party copy s2.
